description: Eastern Irish kingdom (c. 400–1171) centred on modern Leinster whose kings held the Norse Dublin trade network; Diarmait Mac Murchada's invitation of the Anglo-Normans to reclaim his kingdom in 1169 initiated the conquest of Ireland that transformed the island's political landscape under Angevin lordship.

geographic.notes: Centroid approximate; polygon pending schematic or OHM sourcing.

lifecycle_phases.description: Leinster identity consolidates under Uí Dúnlainge dynasty.
Sustained independence as one of the five Irish provinces.
Diarmait invites Normans; Strongbow inherits; Anglo-Norman transformation.

rise_factors.description: Leinster ports, Wexford and Waterford, had active Dublin Norse commercial networks feeding Atlantic and continental trade.
Dublin Norse were partly integrated into Leinster political economy, providing commercial and military capacity.
Wicklow Mountains provided a highland refuge against enemies from the north and west.

Diarmait Mac Murchada's aggressive expansion of Leinster's power through the 12th century made it the most powerful Irish kingdom before his invitation of the Normans, a desperate gambit that transformed Ireland.
Control over Dublin's Norse port gave Leinster access to the most productive trade hub in Ireland, channeling commercial revenues into royal coffers throughout the 11th–12th centuries.

decline_factors.description: Anglo-Norman invasion 1169, invited by Diarmait Mac Murchada, transformed Leinster into the base for Norman conquest of Ireland.
Diarmait's reliance on Strongbow introduced English succession customs that bypassed Irish practice.
Strongbow's inheritance transformed Leinster into an Anglo-Norman lordship.
Richard de Clare (Strongbow) arrived as Diarmait's ally in 1170 and married his daughter, inheriting Leinster on Diarmait's death, the first step in the Norman displacement of Irish royal dynasties.
Henry II of England arrived in 1171 to assert overlordship, receiving submission from both the Norman settlers and Irish kings, creating the Lordship of Ireland that superseded the old kingdoms.
